accessors.name: literal
accessors.note: The plain case, on the lockstep path: a Pike certificate, a linear class, and three finite numbers at every legal length, the stack one always zero because no backtrack stack exists on that path.

accessors.name: nothing-at-all
accessors.note: The empty pattern still prices, so the accessors have answers for a caller who compiled one.

accessors.name: a-large-linear-constant
accessors.note: A counted repetition keeps the backtracking path, and this one is linear with a coefficient near the top of the counter, so the cost answer crosses from finite to ExceedsBudget down the length list while the class stays linear throughout.

accessors.name: a-star-gone-lockstep
accessors.note: On the backtracking path a star is quadratic; compilation routes it to the Pike VM, and the class and the bounds describe the path that will actually run, which is linear.

accessors.name: an-ambiguity-lockstep-defuses
accessors.note: Two identical arms under a star are exponential to a backtracker and nothing at all to a thread list, so what used to be the textbook refusal answers small linear numbers.

accessors.name: polynomial-looking
accessors.note: A counted repetition pins this to the backtracking path, and the star after it makes that path quadratic, so the class is the honest notProvenLinear and the numbers grow with the square.

accessors.name: exponential-looking
accessors.note: A lower bound keeps this off the lockstep path, and the ambiguous body under an unbounded repetition gives the backtracking bound a growing base, so finite numbers at short lengths turn to ExceedsBudget within a few dozen bytes.

accessors.name: ambiguous-no-certificate
accessors.note: A star inside a star can complete an iteration emptily, which keeps it off the lockstep path, and its backtracking bound is a power of a polynomial no certificate can write down. Every accessor refuses: the class too, since a class with no certified bound behind it would be a claim about nothing.

accessors.name: overflowing-no-certificate
accessors.note: One more iteration than the coefficient that fits, on the backtracking path a counted repetition pins it to. The same refusal as above by a different route, and the accessors must not care which.

accessors.name: four-stars-gone-lockstep
accessors.note: The pattern whose backtracking bound needs a power that does not exist, priced finitely anyway, because the path that runs is the thread list and its bound is a closed form in the program size.

analyses.name: literal
analyses.note: Four instructions, no forks, nothing on either growing array. The cost is linear in the subject length because the only thing that repeats is the attempt at each starting position.

analyses.name: nothing-at-all
analyses.note: The empty pattern is one accept under one region, which is the smallest tree there is and still has to price.

analyses.name: capture
analyses.note: Two saves, so a trail where the literal needed none, so a scratch reservation the literal did not pay for.

analyses.name: alternation
analyses.note: A fork costs a backtrack entry, and the certificate says how many: one, whatever the subject is.

analyses.name: an-empty-alternation-branch
analyses.note: The second arm of `(a|)` compiles to nothing, and the branch region for it is still there. A tree the analyzer walked differently from the checker would be refused rather than stored.

analyses.name: optional
analyses.note: One split, whose two arms are the body and what follows it.

analyses.name: star
analyses.note: The head of an unbounded repetition is reached n + 2 times, and the whole of that is run again from every starting position, so the cost is quadratic and the class claim says so.

analyses.name: counted
analyses.note: Bounded above, the declared maximum is what stops it, so there is no term in n inside the loop and the pattern is linear after all.

analyses.name: a-repetition-at-the-declared-maximum
analyses.note: The largest count a quantifier may name. Nothing here is near the counter's range; the numbers are simply large, which is what a caller asking for a budget wanted to know.

analyses.name: grouped-repeat
analyses.note: A capturing group inside a star: the saves are charged per iteration, so the trail grows with the loop rather than with the program.

analyses.name: alternation-inside-a-loop
analyses.note: Two ways round the loop, and nothing in these rules knows that `a` and `b` cannot match the same byte, so the bound is exponential. It overestimates and never underestimates, which is the contract.

analyses.name: exponential
analyses.note: The same shape with the ambiguity written out, where the growing base makes every bound saturate within a few dozen bytes of subject.

analyses.name: nested-unbounded-ambiguity
analyses.note: A star inside a star. The inner one hands the outer one more ways to match at every extra byte, so the pass count is a power of a polynomial and no bound of this shape has that form. The pattern compiles and has no certificate, which is the honest answer.

analyses.name: a-loop-around-a-loop
analyses.note: `(a+)+` the same way, which is the shape a reader is likelier to write than the one above.

analyses.name: the-last-power-that-fits
analyses.note: Each unbounded repetition puts one more power of n on the flow leaving it, and the attempt loop puts on the last. Three in a row is the fourth power, which is the top one a bound has a field for.

analyses.name: one-power-too-many
analyses.note: A fourth is a term with nowhere to go, and dropping it would be the one rounding that goes the wrong way. So there is no certificate rather than a bound missing its largest term.

analyses.name: the-largest-coefficient-that-fits
analyses.note: Two ways round a loop that may go round forty-three times is 2^44 passes, and everything the tree multiplies by that still lands inside a counter.

analyses.name: one-coefficient-too-many
analyses.note: One more time round and it does not. The requirement saturating is not a requirement met, and a coefficient that stopped at the cap is one every claim would be found to satisfy.

analyses.name: a-pass-count-past-the-counter
analyses.note: Far enough out that it is the pass count itself that runs out of room rather than anything derived from it, which is a different place in the arithmetic and gets there its own way.

analyses.name: nested-counted-repetitions
analyses.note: Ten of ten of ten is a hundred iterations of a body that already costs, and the product runs past what a counter holds well before anything about it is ambiguous.

cases.name: literal
cases.note: Three characters and an accept. The whole cost is one visit per instruction at each of the n + 1 starting positions, plus the register file and the ovector, sized and zeroed once, cleared again per attempt, and copied back out when the match is found. That shape is linear, so the certificate says so and the checker holds it to it.

cases.name: capture
cases.note: The same four instructions, two of them saves. A save records an undo entry, so this pattern needs a trail where the literal needed none — which is the whole point of pricing the opcodes rather than counting them.

cases.name: alternation
cases.note: A split, two branches, and the jump the first one leaves by. The region is entered once and both branches are tried, so the ambiguity is two and the accept downstream is charged twice.

cases.name: an-empty-alternation-branch
cases.note: `(a|)` compiles the second branch to nothing at all, so its region covers no instruction. That is legal for a branch and for nothing else: the alternation reads its shape off the branch list, so the branch has to be there whether or not it holds anything.

cases.name: optional
cases.note: One split whose arms are the body and what follows it.

cases.name: lazy-optional
cases.note: The same shape with the split's arms the other way round, which costs exactly the same and is why the rule takes either order.

cases.name: star
cases.note: An unbounded repetition. Past the minimum count an iteration that consumed nothing is the last one, so the head is reached at most n + 2 times and the cost comes out quadratic once the starting positions are counted in.

cases.name: counted
cases.note: A bounded one, where the declared maximum is what stops it and the bound has no term in n at all.

cases.name: grouped-repeat
cases.note: A capturing group inside a star, followed by a literal. The group is entered once per iteration and its saves are charged there, so the trail grows with the loop rather than with the program.

cases.name: alternation-inside-a-loop
cases.note: The same shape with two branches in the group, and the bound comes out exponential. Structurally it is: the loop hands the next iteration one flow per way the body finished, and nothing in these rules knows that `a` and `b` cannot both match the same byte. The bound may overestimate and never underestimate (DESIGN.md section 5), and a first-byte disjointness rule is what would sharpen this one.

cases.name: ambiguous-body-bounded
cases.note: A body with two ways to match the same character, repeated at most three times. Each iteration doubles the ways into the next, so the flow through the head is a power of two and the bound stays a number.

cases.name: exponential
cases.note: The same body with no upper bound, which is where the growing base comes from: the head is reached n + 2 times, so the flow is a multiple of 2^n and the bound saturates within a few dozen bytes of subject. That is the honest answer rather than a number nobody could budget for.

cases.name: a-linear-bound-that-does-not-claim-to-be
cases.note: The class claim of DESIGN.md section 6 may be weaker than the bound, and only weaker. A literal really does cost at most c * (n + 1) and the first case above says so; declining to say so is refusing to make a claim rather than making a wrong one.

cases.name: linear-claim-with-a-square
cases.note: A star does not, and saying so does not make it so.

cases.name: linear-claim-with-a-growing-base
cases.note: Nor does an exponential bound, however small its coefficient.

cases.name: over-claimed-to-both-ceilings
cases.note: A certificate may be generous wherever generosity is legal, and these reach exactly the two ceilings at n = 0: the counter's saturation point for cost and the section 3 byte ceiling for memory. The stack stays exact, because it is held to its equation. What a caller reads back is what the certificate names, not what the checker computed.

cases.name: over-claimed-past-both-ceilings
cases.note: One unit more of each, which no limit could accept, so neither is a number any more. The ceilings differ, which is the whole difference between the projections.

cases.name: a-stack-at-its-ceiling
cases.note: The deepest stack a limit could name, claimed on a program whose derived stack is zero. The evaluation rows still read the claim back as a number at the edge; the checker refuses it, since the stack is held to equality.

cases.name: a-stack-past-its-ceiling
cases.note: One entry more, which no limit could accept, so the evaluation rows refuse it too.

cases.name: past-the-memory-ceiling-and-still-a-cost
cases.note: One IR byte more than the largest reservation there is, claimed as both. It is refused as memory and is a perfectly ordinary amount of work, which is the whole reason the three projections carry their own ceilings rather than sharing the counter's.

cases.name: an-uncaptured-certificate-on-a-capture
cases.note: Four instructions and the same three regions over the same three ranges either way, and the only difference is that two of the instructions are saves. A save records an undo entry, so the certificate for the group that captures nothing is two entries short of the one that does. A checker given only a length could not tell these two programs apart at all.

cases.name: straight-line-certificate-on-a-branching-program
cases.note: Five instructions either way. A split is not an instruction a region may hold loose: the tree has to say which construct it belongs to, or nothing prices the choice it makes.

cases.name: branching-certificate-on-a-straight-line-program
cases.note: And the other way round, where the alternation region is pointed at code that has no split in it.

cases.name: repeat-certificate-on-the-other-repetition
cases.note: Two repetitions, and a region covering the first one's header and the second one's tail. Nothing has to be recorded to make this refusable: each of the four opcodes names its own repetition, and the range pins the head, the body and the exit, so a repeat region cannot be about a quantifier other than the one it covers.

cases.name: configuration-mismatch
cases.note: A certificate for the Pike VM says nothing about the backtracking one, whatever its numbers are.

cases.name: no-rules-for-the-memoized-path
cases.note: The memoized path waits for M9, memo table and all.

cases.name: pike-linear-certificate
cases.note: The closed form itself: no region prices, a linear claim, and the three whole-call numbers of section 9, accepted exactly.

cases.name: pike-linear-certificate-with-captures
cases.note: The same closed form where the counts all bite: two groups widen the block, four Saves multiply the copy-on-write term, and the star stops the program being trivial. Exact, so a restatement that drifted on any of those counts is caught here.

cases.name: pike-claiming-a-stack
cases.note: No backtrack stack exists on the lockstep path, so the stack requirement is exactly zero and the equality rule refuses entries the matcher can never push, under the same name as everywhere.

cases.name: pike-claiming-a-trail
cases.note: Nor does the undo trail exist there, so the trail claim is held to zero by the same equality, under its own name.

cases.name: pike-on-an-ineligible-pattern
cases.note: A lower bound keeps `a+` off the lockstep path, so no Pike certificate can be about it, whatever its numbers say. Refused before anything is priced.

cases.name: pike-for-the-other-configuration
cases.note: A certificate naming the backtracking configuration says nothing here, mirroring the mismatch case above.

cases.name: pike-with-region-prices
cases.note: The Pike form carries no region prices — the visited set makes the whole call a closed form — so a certificate carrying some is a shape the section 9 rules refuse.

cases.name: pike-claiming-less-than-linear
cases.note: Linearity is the shape of the section 9 rule, so a certificate declining to claim it is refused rather than accepted modestly.

cases.name: pike-a-unit-short-on-cost
cases.note: One cost unit under the closed form, refused by name.

cases.name: pike-a-unit-short-on-memory
cases.note: And one IR byte under the reservation.

cases.name: fewer-prices-than-regions
cases.note: A region nobody priced is a region the composition rules would read a zero out of.

cases.name: more-prices-than-regions
cases.note: And a price nobody emitted a region for is a claim about nothing.

cases.name: a-unit-extra-on-stack
cases.note: Cost and memory are bounds and may overestimate; the stack claim is what a preallocated context sizes its backtrack array from, while the memory requirement was priced from the root region's number, so any daylight between the two is refused. One entry above exact, at the constant.

cases.name: a-unit-extra-on-a-growing-stack
cases.note: The same refusal where the stack grows with the subject, one entry above exact at the linear coefficient.

cases.name: a-unit-extra-on-trail
cases.note: The trail is the other array a context sizes, held to its own equation the same way. One undo entry above exact, at the constant, on the pattern whose two saves are the whole trail.

cases.name: a-unit-extra-on-a-growing-trail
cases.note: And where the trail grows with the subject, because the saves sit inside the loop, one entry above exact at the linear coefficient.

cases.name: cost-one-unit-short
cases.note: The setup charge, one unit lower than the register file and the ovector really cost to zero.

cases.name: cost-one-unit-short-per-position
cases.note: The term in n, which is the one that decides whether a long subject fits the budget.

cases.name: cost-one-unit-short-in-the-square
cases.note: And the square, which is a linear loop run from every starting position and is what dominates any subject worth the name.

cases.name: stack-one-entry-short
cases.note: One backtrack entry fewer than the deepest the search goes.

cases.name: trail-one-entry-short
cases.note: One undo entry fewer than the loop records, which the equality refuses from below exactly as it does from above.

cases.name: memory-one-byte-short
cases.note: One IR byte fewer than the peak, which counts the buffer being copied from as well as the one being copied to.

cases.name: memory-one-byte-short-per-position
cases.note: And one byte fewer of the capacity the two growing arrays reach.

cases.name: region-work-one-visit-short
cases.note: The root's own price, a visit short. A region is checked against what its children claim, so this fails at the region rather than at the total it feeds.

cases.name: region-stack-one-entry-short
cases.note: The repetition pushes one entry per pass through its head, and this claims it pushes fewer.

cases.name: region-trail-one-entry-short
cases.note: Its undo entries, which the counter's zeroing, its increment and the position it remembers all fill.

cases.name: region-outs-one-way-short
cases.note: And its ambiguity, one way out short. Understating that would let everything after the loop be priced for fewer passes than it gets.

cases.name: inner-region-work-one-visit-short
cases.note: A group three levels down, a visit short, to show that the induction reaches the leaves rather than stopping at what the root claims.

cases.name: inner-region-trail-one-entry-short
cases.note: And the two saves that group is there for.

cases.name: ambiguity-that-grows-with-the-subject
cases.note: A star inside a star. The inner one hands the outer one more ways to match at every extra byte of subject, so the pass count is a power of a polynomial and no bound of this shape has that form. A refusal is the honest answer.

cases.name: a-pass-count-past-the-counter
cases.note: Two ways round a loop that may go round sixty times is 2^61, which no counter holds. The requirement saturating is not a requirement met.

cases.name: no-regions
cases.note: A certificate with no root has nothing to be the pattern's bound.

cases.name: root-is-not-a-root
cases.note: Region 0 is the root by position, and has to say so as well.

cases.name: root-has-a-parent
cases.note: Nothing encloses the whole program.

cases.name: root-starts-late
cases.note: A root that misses the first instruction prices less than the pattern.

cases.name: root-stops-early
cases.note: And a root that stops short of the last one prices less as well.

cases.name: two-roots
cases.note: Only region 0 is the root, or the tree has two places to start from.

cases.name: parent-above-its-child
cases.note: A parent at or above its child's index is what a cycle looks like from here, and refusing it is what makes the tree a tree without a walk.

cases.name: range-runs-backwards
cases.note: A region that ends before it starts covers no instruction at all.

cases.name: child-outside-its-parent
cases.note: A child reaching past its parent would be priced by neither.

cases.name: child-starts-before-its-parent
cases.note: The other half of the nesting rule, and the reason it is a refusal of its own rather than the sibling one: reaching back before the parent begins is a tree that does not nest, not two children colliding.

cases.name: siblings-overlap
cases.note: Two children sharing an instruction would have it counted twice, or by whichever of them the composition rule reached first.

cases.name: siblings-out-of-order
cases.note: Disjoint but backwards is refused too: the compiler emits regions as it flattens the AST, so source order costs a correct analyzer nothing and lets the checker settle both halves of the sibling rule in one pass.

cases.name: a-bound-with-no-base
cases.note: 0^n is 1 at n = 0 and 0 after that. No bound has that shape, and one that vanishes on longer subjects would look like a bound that holds.

cases.name: a-price-with-no-base
cases.note: The same rule inside the tree, where the composition rules would go on to multiply the thing.

cases.name: a-child-that-covers-nothing
cases.note: A region of zero width prices no instruction and says nothing its parent does not, so the walk never reaches it and it is left over. The compiler drops one rather than emitting it, which is why this tree has to be written by hand.

cases.name: an-alternation-whose-child-is-not-a-branch
cases.note: The branches of an alternation are what its shape is read off, so a child of another kind leaves the split arms unaccounted for.

cases.name: a-branch-outside-an-alternation
cases.note: A branch is one arm of an alternation and means nothing anywhere else. The alternation refuses a child that is not a branch; this is the same rule read from the other end, and between them they say that the two only ever come in pairs.

cases.name: an-alternation-of-one
cases.note: One branch is not an alternation: the compiler emits no split for it, so a region claiming to be one prices instructions that are not there.

cases.name: a-branch-that-does-not-follow-its-split
cases.note: The first branch begins right after the split that guards it. A region starting anywhere else is not the branch that split leads to.

cases.name: a-repeat-over-code-that-repeats-nothing
cases.note: Neither an optional item's split nor a counted repetition's header, so there is no rule to price it with.

cases.name: a-repeat-that-stops-before-its-tail
cases.note: The range of a counted repetition ends where the repetition does. One instruction short of that leaves the tail behind, and the tail is a repetition opcode no region is left to explain.

cases.name: a-repeat-that-reaches-past-its-tail
cases.note: One instruction the other way is a range whose last instruction is not a tail at all, which is what ties a repeat region to the entry in the repetition table.

contexts.name: a-literal-on-the-lockstep-path
contexts.note: The plain case. The reservation is the section 9 closed form made physical — no term in the length at all — and one context answers a match, a no-match, every per-call refusal, and a match again, off the same arrays.

contexts.name: captures-under-a-star
contexts.note: Two matches in a row on the same context, because the ovector is context-owned and the second answer overwrites the first — the documented lifetime, pinned.

contexts.name: a-backtracker-sized-from-its-claims
contexts.note: A counted repetition keeps this on the backtracking path, so the arrays are sized from the certificate's stack and trail claims at the declared length — the reason those claims are held to equality. A stack limit lowered to nothing starves the first fork, and the context is none the worse for it.

contexts.name: the-shortest-context-there-is
contexts.note: A declared maximum of zero is a context for empty subjects, and it still matches them; one byte of subject is past what it was sized for.

contexts.name: no-certificate-no-context
contexts.note: A pattern with no finite bound has no reservation to make, so creation is the same ExceedsBudget the accessors report — after the argument checks, which come first on every pattern.

note: Generated by pcrevera.engine.certificate_corpus. Each case compiles a pattern, hands the engine's bound-certificate checker one certificate for the program that came out, and asks for the three bounds it prices at every subject length below. Each analysis compiles a pattern and reads the certificate the compiler's own analyzer produced, or records that it produced none. Every implementation of the engine has to give exactly these answers: the same verdict, the same class, and the same number or the same refusal. A bound of null is the ExceedsBudget of DESIGN.md section 2.4, which is a refusal rather than a number and never a saturated counter; a complexity of null is a pattern the analyzer found no bound for at all. Each accessor entry asks the public analysis accessors the same questions through each language's wrapper: a status is the outcome ordinal of the engine (0 ok, 3 BadInput, 4 ExceedsBudget), and a query marked exercise must additionally survive a match on a subject of that length with the three pinned bounds passed unchanged as the limits, anything but ResourceExceeded. Each context entry runs its creation ladder through the public context constructor — a memcap, where present, is the reservation the context must materialize, equal to the worstCaseMemory accessor at the declared length — and then replays its calls in order on one context, statuses as match outcome ordinals (0 matched, 1 no match, 2 ResourceExceeded, 3 BadInput); a cost or stack of null is the baked ceiling.
